newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Albright set for emotional visit to Prague.
newsitem.headline: Albright set for emotional visit to Prague.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, on a whirlwind tour of Eastern Europe, arrives in the Czech Republic on Sunday for what is bound to be an emotional visit to the land of her birth.
Albright, after stops in Poland, Slovenia, Russia and Lithuania, visits her birthplace Prague for the first time since becoming the highest ranking woman ever in the U.S. government.

Albright, who speaks Czech, is due to meet Czech Foreign Minister Josef Zieleniec to discuss NATO's invitation this week to the Czech Republic to join the alliance. She will also have a private dinner with President Vaclav Havel.
After this week's NATO summit in Madrid, Albright said she was pleased with the invitations to Poland and Hungary but the call to the Czech Republic had warmed her heart.
"It makes me feel that I've been part of history," she said.
Zieleniec told a news conference on Friday Albright's visit would be an important stage in the process of negotiations towards NATO membership.
"The Madrid summit...is the beginning of something new, a qualitatively different stage and I am glad that that period starts with the visit of the Secretary of State.
"It will be very important in which way we formulate, in the course of her visit, the starting point for the political process of negotiations," Zieleniec said.
But beyond affairs of state, Albright's visit is a homecoming.
She still has a cousin in the Czech Republic but it was not clear whether they would meet.

However, she is scheduled to walk on Monday from the palatial Foreign Ministry, where her father, a Czechoslovak diplomat, used to work, to Prague Castle and will pass the house where she lived as a small girl.
Prague has long seen Albright as a strong supporter of Czech membership of NATO and as a powerful friend.
On Monday, she is to receive the Order of the White Lion, the highest Czech civilian honour.
Albright's family fled the former Czechoslovakia twice, once to escape the Nazis and then, in 1948, the communists.

Her father, Josef Korbel, was a diplomat who served with the World War Two government-in-exile in London and who later was given political asylum in the United States, where he settled with his family.

Revelations about Albright's origins caused a flurry in February when the Washington Post, researching her background, found she appeared to be of Jewish ancestry and that three of her grandparents had died in the Holocaust.
A White House spokesman said at the time that Albright had believed from an early age she was Roman Catholic and was only now coming to understand her heritage was Jewish.
She will also deliver a speech at Prague's art deco Municipal House, recently restored to its original splendour.
As an academic, Albright advised Havel, a former dissident playwright, after the 1989 "Velvet Revolution" which ended 40 years of communism in Czechoslovakia.
Later, as U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, she joined Havel in a smoky Prague jazz club to hear U.S. President Bill Clinton play the saxophone during a 1995 state visit.
